about: Homestead data for the Sphere's farm layer, western Washington: the work around the planting calendar — cover crops, the last sowings for a winter harvest, season extension, harvest storage, beginner seed saving, and small seasonal notes for chickens and goats. Every entry carries the source it came from, and only extension and university sources are used: WSU Extension, Oregon State's PNW 548, and the extension services of Nebraska, Kansas State, Illinois, North Carolina State, Wisconsin, and Penn State, with NOAA frost normals for the two founding counties. Where sources disagree, the disagreement is written into the entry rather than smoothed over. A category with no solid source behind it is left out, never guessed. WSU's cover crop table speaks in parts of months (beginning, mid, end); this dataset renders beginning as days 1–10, mid as 11–20, and end or late as day 21 to the month's end, and the words govern.

locations.anchor: Morton–Centralia lowland, and the Randle valley floor
locations.frostRangeNote: The NOAA median (the middle year of 1991–2020) says last spring frost Apr 22 and first fall frost Oct 27. The Old Farmer's Almanac, counting a 30% chance of frost after the date instead, says Apr 30 and Oct 19. The median plans the season; the Almanac line is the safer one.

WSU's Snohomish weather station has recorded last spring frosts from Mar 18 to May 1 since 2012, so the frost watch here stays open until May 1 even though the lowland median is Mar 24. First fall frosts on the same record run from Oct 4 to Nov 19.

coverCrops.name: Cereal rye
coverCrops.purpose: Nitrogen scavenger, quick cover, rapid spring growth, and competes with weeds
notes: Hardy and reliable — one of the most commonly grown cover crops in the Northwest.
It grows rapidly in the spring, so mow or cut it before turning it under, or it can be hard to incorporate.

coverCrops.name: Crimson clover
coverCrops.purpose: Legume nitrogen source, soil builder, erosion fighter
notes: Easy to incorporate when its season ends.

coverCrops.name: Hairy vetch
notes: A reliable legume. WSU's mixture table pairs it with cereal rye (1/4 cup rye and 3/4 cup vetch per 100 sq ft); it germinates in the fall but grows slowly until spring.

coverCrops.name: Winter wheat
coverCrops.purpose: Nitrogen scavenger, soil builder, quick cover, rapid spring growth
notes: Most suitable for mid- to late-season planting; planting it before late September makes it more susceptible to disease and premature death.

coverCrops.name: Winter oats
coverCrops.purpose: Nitrogen scavenger, quick cover, rapid spring growth, competes with weeds
notes: Spring oat varieties (such as Cayuse and Monida) should be planted by early September in the Puget Sound area to get good growth.

coverCrops.name: Annual ryegrass
coverCrops.purpose: Nitrogen scavenger, soil builder, quick cover, rapid spring growth
notes: Tolerates wet soils, and its vigorous roots reduce erosion.

finalSowings.note: WSU Clallam County's fall and winter chart (adapted from PNW 548) is written for the North Olympic Peninsula; it is WSU's maritime western-Washington guidance and is kept here in the chart's own months. Most winter crops in it are planted from mid-July through August and must be well established by the first frost.

seasonExtension.name: Cold frames and low tunnels over the winter crops
seasonExtension.text: Covering winter crops with a cold frame or row cover protects them from frost, heavy rain, and cold winds, and protection from rain alone can extend the life of a winter garden dramatically. Covers should be in place before the county's frost window opens.

seasonExtension.name: Cold frames for seed starting and hardening off
seasonExtension.text: Cold frames earn their keep in the spring frost window: they are used for starting seeds and for hardening off plants before they go into the garden, and they grow cool-season crops like lettuce, radishes, and spinach well. Ventilate the frame when temperatures rise above 45°F inside it.

seasonExtension.name: Covers off and stored
seasonExtension.text: The latest spring frost on this county's record has passed. Season extenders can come off and be stored; WSU's Skagit gardeners count them good for two to four extra weeks at each end of the season, spring and fall.

seasonExtension.name: The winter garden is planted in summer
seasonExtension.text: Most winter crops are planted from mid-July through August — late enough that they will not mature too early in the warm months, early enough to be well established by the first frost.

storage.note: The panel speaks storage in the harvest months (September to November), when these crops come in. Conditions are the extension tables' own figures; where two tables differ, both are kept and the entry says so.

crops.name: Onions, dry
crops.cureText: Cure first: spread in a single layer on a screen or in a well-ventilated area for 2–4 weeks before storing.
notes: Keep onions away from apples and potatoes — onions and peppers can impart off-flavors to both in storage.

crops.name: Garlic
crops.cureText: Cure first: spread in a single layer or tie in bunches in a shaded, well-ventilated, cool area for 2–4 weeks.

crops.name: Potatoes, late crop
crops.cureText: Cure first, in a dark place for 1–2 weeks. WSU counts the curing warmth at 50–65°F; Nebraska's curing table counts 60–70°F. The range is kept.
notes: Late-crop potatoes are the keepers; early potatoes do not store as long.
Kansas State's table gives 4–5 months at 40°F, inside Nebraska's wider 2–9 months.
Keep potatoes away from apples — apple gas makes potatoes sprout.

crops.name: Winter squash
crops.cureText: Cure first (all but acorn squash): 80–85°F for 7–14 days to harden the skins.
notes: Cool and dry is its corner of the cellar — the warmest of the four storage groups WSU names.

crops.name: Apples
notes: Kansas State's table allows 1–12 months depending on the variety; Nebraska's 3–8 months is the home-storage planning range kept here.
Apples give off ethylene gas. WSU's word: avoid storing apples or pears with celery, cabbage, carrots, potatoes, or onions.

seedSaving.note: Beginner seed saving, from the crops that pollinate themselves. Save seed only from open-pollinated varieties — seed from hybrids will not grow true to the parent. The panel speaks seed saving from August through October, when these crops ripen and dry down.

crops.name: Beans
crops.isolationText: Keep 10–20 feet between varieties (Illinois Extension's chart); NC State says at least 10 feet.
crops.howText: Let the pods mature and dry on the vine. Collect them before they split and let them dry 1–2 weeks more before shelling.

crops.name: Peas
crops.isolationText: Keep 10–20 feet between varieties (Illinois Extension's chart); NC State says at least 10 feet.
crops.howText: Let the pods mature and dry on the vine. Collect them before they split and let them dry 1–2 weeks more before shelling.

crops.name: Lettuce
crops.isolationText: Keep 10–20 feet between varieties (Illinois Extension's chart).
crops.howText: Beans, peas, and lettuce are the crops Illinois Extension names as not requiring isolation — a few plants give good seed.

crops.name: Tomatoes
crops.isolationText: NC State counts 20–30 feet between varieties if you can; Illinois counts a few rows apart. Both are kept.
crops.howText: Cut a fully ripe fruit and squeeze the pulp into a container with a little water. Let it ferment at room temperature 3–4 days, stirring daily; the good seed settles out. Rinse it and spread it thin to dry thoroughly.

animals.note: Small seasonal notes only, from extension livestock guidance. No WSU goat calendar was found, so the goat note rests on Penn State Extension and says so in its entry.

entries.name: Winterize the coop before winter
lines: Chickens need a dry, draft-free, and well-ventilated building. Put down 6–12 inches of dry bedding on the floor for insulation.
Water is the winter problem: birds need access at least every 10 hours, day and night. Keep it from freezing with a heater in the waterer or a heated bowl.
Birds eat more in winter to stay warm. Feed a good balanced diet, free-choice if you can, or scatter high-energy feed like grains or oilseeds in the coop in the evening.
Large combs and wattles can frostbite; a little petroleum jelly on them reduces the chance.

entries.name: Light, if you want eggs through winter
lines: Hens need 14–16 hours of light to keep laying. If you add light, Wisconsin Extension counts it as traditionally started around September 1 and kept up until spring's natural day length reaches 14 hours.
It is a choice, not a duty — hens also rest and molt when the days shorten.

entries.name: Winter care for does (Penn State Extension — no WSU goat calendar was found)
lines: Give the herd a well-ventilated, draft-free shelter with ample bedding, and keep does dry — wet and cold together are what hurt them.
Watch body condition through winter and aim for 2.5 to 3.5 on the 5-point score; adjust feed before a doe falls below it.

A doe in her last trimester is growing about 70% of the kid in those weeks and needs more energy and protein — Penn State counts 0.5 to 1 pound of a 12–14% protein grain a day as common, rising toward kidding.
